Amanda, good to meet you. I am Martin Reis, from the legal team here. Tell me where you are now.
I am the legal manager of an agribusiness group, and I have been there for four years.
Four years. And before that? I would rather hear the story than read the profile.
I started in a law firm in two thousand and thirteen, and I stayed for three years. Then I moved in-house, and I have never gone back.
Why not? Most people go the other way when the money is better.
Because in a firm I wrote the opinion and somebody else decided. In-house I am in the room, and I sign off on the contract myself.
Fair. Tell me about one contract that went wrong.
In two thousand and twenty-two a buyer stopped paying. The jurisdiction clause sent us abroad, so the case was slow and expensive. Since then I have read that clause first, in every contract.
That is the answer I was hoping for. Have you ever worked on a carbon project?
Not yet. But I have spent eleven years on contracts in a sector that lives on land, and the regulation is where the work is going.

Hi Amanda, this is Martin Reis from the legal team. Thanks for making time on Friday. I wanted to give you a heads up about the call so that nothing takes you by surprise. It is a conversation, not an interview, and it lasts about thirty minutes. I have read your profile already, so please do not repeat it line by line. What I am interested in is the story behind it: where you started, why you moved from the law firm to the company side, and what you have been doing since you took over the department. I will also ask about one contract that went wrong, because that is where I learn the most about a lawyer. And bring questions for me. Half of the call is yours. See you on Friday.

So, my name is Helena Duarte and this is the short version. I studied law in Porto Alegre and I joined a firm in my second year, which is where I learned to draft. I stayed for six years and I loved almost none of it, because I never met the client twice. In two thousand and seventeen I moved in-house, to a food company, and everything changed: suddenly I was in the room where the decision happened. I have been in-house ever since. I have worked on supply contracts, on two acquisitions and, for the last three years, on environmental compliance, which nobody in my team wanted and which turned out to be the most interesting work I have ever done. If you are thinking about the same move, my advice is simple. Go where the decision is made.

Start with where you are now and how long you have been there. Then go back to the beginning and say where you studied and where you started. Then say what you did in each step, with the dates. Then say what has changed since you took over the department. And finally, say what you want next and why.
